claims.text: Brittle behavior in an initially single-phase, compositionally complex high-entropy alloy emerges primarily from thermally activated grain-boundary short-range order rather than conventional precipitation.
Grain-boundary short-range ordering reduces grain-boundary cohesion.
Reduced grain-boundary cohesion leads to toughness degradation under thermal and mechanical loading.
The proposed initial material is a homogeneous, single-phase high-entropy alloy with minimal preexisting grain-boundary ordering.
Slower cooling promotes grain-boundary short-range ordering.
Faster cooling suppresses grain-boundary short-range ordering.
Prolonged aging allows local chemical ordering to develop at grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary ordering promotes intergranular crack initiation and propagation.
Intergranular crack initiation and propagation manifest as brittle behavior.
Slow-cooled, extended-aged specimens will have more grain-boundary short-range order than rapidly quenched specimens.
The proposed grain-boundary short-range order can be detected by TEM or atom-probe tomography.
Slow-cooled, extended-aged specimens will exhibit lower tensile ductility than rapidly quenched specimens.
Slow-cooled, extended-aged specimens will exhibit lower fracture toughness than rapidly quenched specimens.
Rapid cooling produces a baseline with less short-range order and higher toughness and ductility.
Temperature-induced ductility loss can occur in a single-phase FCC high-entropy alloy without intermetallic formation because elemental segregation causes grain-boundary decohesion.
Slow cooling can coarsen gamma-prime particles and produce serrated grain boundaries that improve tensile fracture strain and creep rupture life.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts that slow cooling degrades ductility and toughness by promoting grain-boundary order, whereas cited record PMC9848264 reports that slow cooling promotes serrated grain boundaries and substantially improves tensile fracture strain and creep rupture life through reduced strain concentration and resistance to intergranular cracking.
The design describes thermally aged specimens subsequently tested mechanically, but the rule refers to 'mechanically aged specimens,' creating ambiguity about which treatment is being evaluated.
